text: I think that letters hold a very special value, even in this age of instant messaging. The fact that it is slow, it is a different format. People writing by hand is different because of the handwriting itself. It's more personal, it's very specific to that person. So there is something very intimate about handwriting, the pressure that you put into writing. If you cross out something, and you correct it, you actually see the person in that message. The fact that it takes time, it's different. You choose your paper, you buy the stamp, you send it. And then you wait for the reply, which can take days. That gives value to what you write. There's a commitment there. Letters are a physical object. You can keep them, you can fold them, you can reread them. They are tangible. And you can find them 10 years later and reread them. And it's different from digital, because you can lose digital messages or bury them. A letter, if you keep it, it's there. You can come back to it and reread it, be in a very quiet moment, and just focus on the letters. Letters are also slow, which encourages you to reflect on what you want to say.
